stories.title_en: How close can pure functional programming get to C?

comments.author: jandrewrogers
comments.text:
Much of the difference in optimizability is that C/C++ allows you to do fairly extreme copy elision. This is important because memory bandwidth tends to be a major performance bottleneck.
C/C++ code can trivially reach into some remote bit of state and mutate it directly. The compiler rarely objects, no matter how ugly the access method or pattern. It is up to the programmer to make sure the invariants hold and the compiler can’t always see through it. These elided copies add up, though it usually has a maintainability and safety cost.
It is related to why functional languages tend to be mediocre for supercomputing in practice despite having nice properties for massive parallelism in theory.

Nice article. There's another option for pixel art that's recently been coming into vogue as tool usage improves in LLMs which is procedural graphics.
I actually experimented with creating a set of skills around rendering early AGI style EGA graphical scenes, and it worked surprisingly well.
So rather than storing full bitmaps, you instead store sequences of simple drawing instructions designed to recreate some specific scene - like you would an SVG.
As a result you end up sidestepping a lot of the problems with larger generative models, which can have issues with grid alignment, palette choices, and high-frequency noise.

The whole point is to keep rows physically close, so you can very quickly extract an entire time range from a number of database shards, with minimal reads and compute. Kind of funny title since I didn’t think UUIDv7 had any of the properties being disputed here. The reason to use UUIDv7 is because it reduces the space over which the UUID can cover at a given time, which improves write clustering. comments.author: sedatk
comments.text:

https://ssg.dev/you-probably-dont-need-a-uuid/

comments.author: rcoder
comments.text:
If you really need monotonic, secure/unguessable IDs, there are options like CUID2 (github.com/paralleldrive/cuid2).
Older designs like ULIDs (
https://github.com/ulid/spec
) and Snowflake IDs (
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowflake_ID
) have similar properties to UUIDv7, and potentially some advantages w.r.t. length/encoding/runtime cost/etc.
But UUIDv7 has one key advantage none of those do: you can store them in a UUID-typed column or struct field without any lossy conversion. All of the UUID versions share a common size and serialization format, so it doesn't actually matter if you generate v1/4/7/etc.
Many language standard libraries can generate them interchangeably, and (for example) a Postgres table can store any of the versions in the same column type.
So yes, to the author's point(s): they are not magic, monotonic, un-guessable IDs and you shouldn't treat them as either "secure" or strictly ordered. That doesn't mean they aren't useful.
